claim: Prokaryotes utilize polycistronic messages (operons) to co-translate proteins involved in the same biological processes.
source: Prokaryotes utilize polycistronic messages (operons) to co-translate proteins involved in the same biological processes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about prokaryotic gene organization and expression.

claim: mRNAs encoding components of the mating pathway, heat shock proteins, and mitochondrial outer membrane proteins multiplex in trans, forming discrete messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes (called transperons).
source: Consistent with the hypothesis of eukaryotic RNA operons, mRNAs encoding components of the mating pathway, heat shock proteins, and mitochondrial outer membrane proteins multiplex in trans, forming discrete messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes (called transperons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RaPID-seq, RaPID-qPCR, and smFISH experiments shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Genes encoding multiplexed mRNAs physically interact.
source: Chromatin capture and allele tagging experiments reveal that genes encoding multiplexed mRNAs physically interact; thus, RNA assembly may result from co-regulated gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin conformation capture (3C) experiments and live cell imaging of tagged genomic loci shown in Figure 7.

claim: Transperon assembly and function depends upon histone H4.
source: Transperon assembly and function depends upon histone H4, and its depletion leads to defects in RNA multiplexing, decreased pheromone responsiveness and mating, and increased heat shock sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-MS identification of Hhf1, immunoprecipitation experiments, deletion studies, and auxin-induced depletion experiments shown in Figures 3-5 and Figure 8.

claim: Histone H4 depletion leads to defects in RNA multiplexing.
source: Transperon assembly and function depends upon histone H4, and its depletion leads to defects in RNA multiplexing, decreased pheromone responsiveness and mating, and increased heat shock sensitivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RaPID-qPCR experiments in hhf deletion mutants and auxin-induced depletion strains shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 8.

claim: Histone H4 depletion leads to decreased pheromone responsiveness and mating.
source: Transperon assembly and function depends upon histone H4, and its depletion leads to defects in RNA multiplexing, decreased pheromone responsiveness and mating, and increased heat shock sensitivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative mating assays and shmooing efficiency measurements shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 6.

claim: Histone H4 depletion leads to increased heat shock sensitivity.
source: Transperon assembly and function depends upon histone H4, and its depletion leads to defects in RNA multiplexing, decreased pheromone responsiveness and mating, and increased heat shock sensitivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays measuring doubling time after heat shock shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Intergenic associations and non-canonical histone H4 functions contribute to transperon formation in eukaryotic cells and regulate cell physiology.
source: We propose that intergenic associations and non-canonical histone H4 functions contribute to transperon formation in eukaryotic cells and regulate cell physiology.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including chromatin capture, histone H4 binding to mRNAs, and physiological effects of H4 depletion.

claim: Eukaryotic operons have been observed to give rise to dicistronic messages in C. elegans.
source: However, this mode of action has not been reported in eukaryotes, except for a few limited examples (e.g., in Caenorhabditis elegans [C. elegans]) (Spieth et al., 1993), and eukaryotic operons have been observed to give rise to dicistronic messages (Blumenthal, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature (Spieth et al., 1993; Blumenthal, 2004).

claim: Eukaryotic messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) particles are composed of multiple RNAs and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs).
source: One possibility is that eukaryotic messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) particles, which are composed of multiple RNAs and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) (Mitchell and Parker, 2014), effectively confer combinatorial gene expression networks similar to prokaryotic operons (Keene and Tenenbaum, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature (Mitchell and Parker, 2014).

claim: Genomic DNA folds create sites of transcriptional hot spots.
source: Although the mechanism remains unknown, studies have shown that genomic DNA folds create sites of transcriptional hot spots (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2014) that could facilitate multiplexing by co-localizing messages during transcription and coordinating the subsquent association of RBPs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2014).

claim: Extensive interactions can occur directly between RNAs in living cells.
source: Moreover, RNA-RNA interactome studies show that extensive interactions can occur directly between RNAs in living cells (Aw et al., 2016; Engreitz et al., 2014; Kudla et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Aw et al., 2016; Engreitz et al., 2014; Kudla et al., 2011; Nguyen et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016).

claim: Individual yeast RBPs have been shown to bind to numerous (e.g., 10s-1000s) mRNAs.
source: Although individual yeast RBPs have been shown to bind to numerous (e.g., 10s-1000s) mRNAs (Hogan et al., 2008), these RNA-binding studies are based primarily upon crosslinking and RBP pulldowns that are unable to define the minimal number of mRNA species in a single mRNP particle.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature (Hogan et al., 2008).

claim: RaPID-seq identifies MS2-tagged target mRNAs.
source: We have previously demonstrated that RaPID-seq identifies MS2-tagged target mRNAs (Haimovich et al., 2016) and now show here that additional messages associate with these transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Haimovich et al., 2016) and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Select MS2-labeled target mRNAs (e.g., SRO7, EXO70, OM45) co-precipitated untagged mRNAs encoding secreted proteins involved in cell mating (e.g., STE3, SAG1, MFα1, MFα2) in MATα yeast.
source: By employing MATα yeast in RaPID-seq pulldown experiments, we found that select MS2-labeled target mRNAs (e.g., SRO7, EXO70, OM45) co-precipitated untagged mRNAs encoding secreted proteins involved in cell mating (e.g., STE3, SAG1, MFα1, MFα2).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-seq data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: A corresponding complex (e.g., STE2, AGA1, AGA2, MFA1, MFA2) could be precipitated from MATa cells.
source: Since a corresponding complex (e.g., STE2, AGA1, AGA2, MFA1, MFA2) could also be precipitated from MATa cells, it suggested to us that mRNAs encoding secreted proteins involved in mating (e.g., pheromones, pheromone receptors, agglutinins, and proteases) multiplex into a functionally selective mRNP complex – the mating transperon.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Yeast histone H4 paralogs, Hhf1 and Hhf2, interact with mating mRNAs to regulate complex assembly.
source: We found that the yeast histone H4 paralogs, Hhf1 and Hhf2 (Dollard et al., 1994), interact with these mRNAs to regulate complex assembly.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-MS data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3C, E).

claim: Pheromone responsiveness (e.g., shmooing) and mating were inhibited by either histone H4 depletion or a block in H4 acetylation.
source: Furthermore, both pheromone responsiveness (e.g., shmooing) and mating were inhibited by either histone H4 depletion or a block in H4 acetylation.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assays and shmooing efficiency measurements shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: No other histones had the effect on mating when mutated.
source: When mutated, no other histones had this effect.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assays of histone deletion mutants shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Conserved cis elements exist in the mating mRNAs.
source: Moreover, we could identify conserved cis elements in the mating mRNAs and demonstrate that mutations therein had deleterious effects on mRNA multiplexing, pheromone responsiveness, and mating, which were similar to those seen upon histone H4 mutation.
evidence: This is supported by MEME analysis (Figure 6A) and experimental data showing effects of motif mutations (Figure 6B, C).

claim: Mutations in conserved cis elements in mating mRNAs had deleterious effects on mRNA multiplexing, pheromone responsiveness, and mating.
source: Moreover, we could identify conserved cis elements in the mating mRNAs and demonstrate that mutations therein had deleterious effects on mRNA multiplexing, pheromone responsiveness, and mating, which were similar to those seen upon histone H4 mutation.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR, mating assays, and shmooing efficiency measurements shown in Figure 6B, C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A specific interaction between the STE2 and AGA2 genes was identified in MATa cells.
source: Importantly, a specific interaction between the STE2 and AGA2 genes was identified in MATa cells, which suggests that interallelic coupling may give rise to RNA multiplexing.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin conformation capture (3C) data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Allelic coupling appeared to occur in both a transcription- and histone H4-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, coupling appeared to occur in both a transcription- and histone H4-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging experiments with transcription inhibitor treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) and in hhf1Δ cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).

claim: HSP genes undergo intergenic interactions during heat shock.
source: To help validate this hypothesis, we examined whether mRNAs encoding heat shock proteins (HSPs), whose genes were previously shown to undergo intergenic interactions during heat shock (Chowdhary et al., 2019), also undergo multiplexing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature (Chowdhary et al., 2019).

claim: HSP mRNAs multiplex in trans during heat shock to form RNP complexes.
source: Importantly, HSP mRNAs were found to multiplex in trans during heat shock to form RNP complexes, and histone H4 was required for both RNA multiplexing and robust post-heat shock cell recovery.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data (Figure 8A) and smFISH co-localization data (Figure 8B, C).

claim: Histone H4 was required for both HSP RNA multiplexing and robust post-heat shock cell recovery.
source: Importantly, HSP mRNAs were found to multiplex in trans during heat shock to form RNP complexes, and histone H4 was required for both RNA multiplexing and robust post-heat shock cell recovery.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR in H4 depletion strains (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, B) and growth assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Additional RNA multiplexes exist for mitochondrial outer membrane proteins and MAP kinase pathway proteins in yeast.
source: Parallel studies revealed the existence of additional RNA multiplexes for mitochondrial outer membrane proteins and MAP kinase pathway proteins in yeast.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data (Figure 9A, D) and smFISH co-localization data (Figure 9B, C, E, F).

claim: Histone H4-mediated chromatin interactions may lead to the formation of functionally selective transperons in eukaryotic cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that histone H4-mediated chromatin interactions may lead to the formation of functionally selective transperons in eukaryotic cells and possibly act as a means to co-regulate gene expression in place of polycistronicity.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the integration of multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: RaPID allows for a biochemical view of the protein and RNA constituents of mRNPs at the single transcript level.
source: Unlike CLIP or PAR-CLIP, which collects information on all RBP-RNA interactions in the cell and is biased toward highly expressed mRNAs with long poly-A tails (Hafner et al., 2010), RaPID allows for a biochemical view of the protein and RNA constituents of mRNPs at the single transcript level.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citation to published literature (Hafner et al., 2010) and the description of the RaPID method.

claim: RaPID employs the precipitation of MS2 aptamer-tagged messages using the MCP fused to streptavidin-binding peptide, followed by elution from immobilized streptavidin with free biotin.
source: RaPID employs the precipitation of MS2 aptamer-tagged messages using the MCP fused to streptavidin-binding peptide, followed by elution from immobilized streptavidin with free biotin, and then mass spectrometry (Slobodin and Gerst, 2010; Slobodin and Gerst, 2011) or RNA-seq (Haimovich et al., 2016) to identify bound proteins and RNAs, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations to published literature (Slobodin and Gerst, 2010; Slobodin and Gerst, 2011; Haimovich et al., 2016).

claim: Non-tagged RNAs co-precipitated with MS2-tagged target mRNAs included retrotransposable elements (e.g., Ty elements), tRNAs, ribosomal RNAs, telomere and small nuclear RNAs.
source: These included retrotransposable elements (e.g., Ty elements), tRNAs, ribosomal RNAs, telomere and small nuclear RNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and coding RNAs (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Five mRNAs encoding secreted and membrane proteins (mSMPs) of the mating process were found associated with a subset of target RNAs.
source: Notably, five mRNAs encoding secreted and membrane proteins (mSMPs) of the mating process were found associated with a subset of target RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-seq data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Target transcripts consisted of two cER-localized mRNAs that encode polarity factors (mPOLs; SRO7 and EXO70) and OM45, an mRNA that encodes a mitochondrial outer membrane protein (MOMP).
source: These target transcripts consisted of two cER-localized mRNAs that encode polarity factors (mPOLs; SRO7 and EXO70) (Aronov et al., 2007) and OM45, an mRNA that encodes a mitochondrial outer membrane protein (MOMP), which we have shown to localize to both mitochondria and ER (Gadir et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature (Aronov et al., 2007; Gadir et al., 2011).

claim: Co-precipitated non-tagged mRNAs included STE3, MFα1, MFα2, SAG1, and AFB1.
source: Co-precipitated non-tagged mRNAs included STE3, which encodes the a-pheromone receptors, MFα1 and MFα2, which both encode α-mating factor, SAG1, which encodes α-agglutinin, and AFB1, which encodes the a-pheromone blocker (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The corresponding MATa mating-type RNAs (e.g., STE2, MFA1, MFA2, AGA2, and BAR1) were negatively enriched (depleted) in pulldowns from MATα cells.
source: Importantly, the corresponding MATa mating-type RNAs (e.g., STE2, MFA1, MFA2, AGA2, and BAR1), as well as other MATa RNAs involved in mating (e.g., STE6, ASG7), were negatively enriched (depleted) in these pulldowns (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-seq data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The pulldown of SAG1 mRNA co-precipitated cohort mRNAs of the mating pathway (e.g., MFα1, MFα2), but not unrelated mRNAs (e.g., UBC6, WSC2).
source: We verified the RaPID-Seq results using RaPID followed by qRT-PCR (RaPID-qPCR) and found that the pulldown of SAG1 mRNA co-precipitated cohort mRNAs of the mating pathway (e.g., MFα1, MFα2), but not unrelated mRNAs (e.g., UBC6, WSC2) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The precipitation of AGA1 mRNA led to co-precipitation of cohort mating pathway mRNAs (e.g., STE2, AGA2, MFA1, MFA2) in MATa cells.
source: Indeed, the precipitation of AGA1 mRNA using RaPID led to co-precipitation of the cohort mating pathway mRNAs (e.g., STE2, AGA2, MFA1, MFA2; Figure 2B), along with SRO7.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Endogenously expressed MS2-tagged STE2 and AGA1 mRNAs co-localized either with nER or with cER, both with or without α-factor.
source: We found that both mRNAs co-localized either with nER or with cER, both with or without α-factor (images for mCherry-Scs2 are shown in Figure 2C and quantified for mCherry-Sec63 in Figure 2D), and are not present in the bud or shmoo tips (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: MFA1 and MFA2 mRNAs localized to the cell bodies in either pheromone-treated and non-treated cells.
source: Both MFA1 and MFA2 mRNAs localized to the cell bodies in either pheromone-treated and non-treated cells, and no difference in localization was observed upon the deletion of SHE2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 65.5 ± 7.7% of PP7-tagged AGA2 mRNA co-localized with MS2-tagged STE2 mRNA.
source: Overall, we found that 65.5 ± 7.7% (average ± standard deviation; n = 3 experiments) of PP7-tagged AGA2 mRNA co-localized with MS2-tagged STE2 mRNA (Figure 2D), of which 39.5 ± 3.5% co-localized in the cytoplasm and 60.5 ± 3.5% co-localized in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 73.1 ± 1.0% of STE2 mRNA spots co-localized with PP7-tagged AGA2 mRNA spots in untreated cells.
source: The majority (73.1 ± 1.0%) of STE2 mRNA spots co-localized with PP7-tagged AGA2 mRNA spots in untreated cells, while 65.4 ± 0.1% co-localized in cells treated with α-factor (Figure 2E and F), and co-localization was observed both in the nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: 37.9 ± 1.7% of AGA1 mRNA co-localized with STE2 mRNA.
source: Overall, we found that 37.9 ± 1.7% (average ± standard error of the mean; SEM) of AGA1 mRNA co-localized with STE2 mRNA, while only 9.8 ± 0.6% of HSP150 mRNA co-localized with STE2 mRNA (Figure 3A and B; representative images are shown in Figure 3a and quantified in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Only 9.8 ± 0.6% of HSP150 mRNA co-localized with STE2 mRNA.
source: Overall, we found that 37.9 ± 1.7% (average ± standard error of the mean; SEM) of AGA1 mRNA co-localized with STE2 mRNA, while only 9.8 ± 0.6% of HSP150 mRNA co-localized with STE2 mRNA (Figure 3A and B; representative images are shown in Figure 3a and quantified in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: A band of ~150 kDa was present in all RaPID-MS lanes, except for the lanes corresponding to STE2 mRNA lacking its 3'UTR and ASH1 mRNA.
source: We identified a band of ~150 kDa that was present in all lanes upon silver staining, except for the lanes corresponding to STE2 mRNA lacking its 3'UTR and ASH1 mRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sequencing revealed that the ~150 kDa band contained a core histone H4 paralog, Hhf1.
source: Sequencing revealed that this band contained a core histone H4 paralog, Hhf1.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry sequencing of the band from RaPID-MS experiments.

claim: HA-Hhf1 could precipitate either native or MS2 aptamer-tagged STE2, along with native MFA1 or MFA2 mRNA, but not EXO70, ASH1, SRO7, or UBC6 mRNA.
source: First, we found that HA-Hhf1 could precipitate either native or MS2 aptamer-tagged STE2, along with native MFA1 or MFA2 mRNA, but not EXO70, ASH1, SRO7, or UBC6 mRNA by RT-PCR (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HA-Hhf1 migrates at around 12 kDa in SDS-PAGE gels.
source: Thus, we could verify a specific interaction between Hhf1 and RNAs of the mating particle and, in addition, show that HA-Hhf1 migrates at around 12 kDa in SDS-PAGE gels (Figure 3D), as predicted.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: HA-Hhf1 pulldowns could detect native STE2, MFA1, and MFA2, but not SRO7 or WSC2, in the precipitates by qRT-PCR.
source: Next, we validated these results in HA-Hhf1 pulldowns using qRT-PCR, whereby we could detect native STE2, MFA1, and MFA2, but not SRO7 or WSC2, in the precipitates (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only deletions in H4 (hhf1Δ or hhf2Δ) led to a significant decrease (~50–60%) in mating.
source: We found that only deletions in H4 (hhf1Δ or hhf2Δ) led to a significant decrease (~50–60%) in mating (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Growth of AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells in presence of 3-IAA resulted in a full depletion of Hhf1 within 4 hr.
source: Growth of the cells in presence of 3-IAA resulted in a full depletion of Hhf1 within 4 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and cells remained viable after this short-term treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and growth assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Depletion of histone H4 resulted in >80% inhibition in mating after pre-treatment with 3-IAA (4 mM; 4 hr).
source: When examined for mating after pre-treatment with 3-IAA (4 mM; 4 hr), we observed a >80% inhibition in mating (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Auxin treatment does not abolish the increase in mating mRNA levels observed upon pheromone addition.
source: In the cases of STE2 and AGA1, we observed similar increases in mRNA transcript levels in either cell type upon α-factor addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) with or without added 3-IAA. Thus, auxin treatment does not abolish the increase in mating mRNA levels observed upon pheromone addition.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Co-localization of AGA1 and STE2 mRNAs was reduced in AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells upon auxin treatment.
source: While WT cells gave 37.9 ± 1.7% co-localization, this was reduced to 15.9 ± 1.0 and 14.0 ± 0.9% (avg. ± SEM) either without or with 3-IAA addition, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Decreased levels of AGA1, AGA2, and, to a lesser degree, MFA1 mRNA were found in the hhfΔ deletion strains by RaPID-PCR.
source: We first performed RaPID-PCR on STE2 mRNA derived from hhf1Δ and hhf2Δ cells, and measured the co-precipitation of other mating pathway mRNAs. We found decreased levels of AGA1, AGA2, and, to a lesser degree, MFA1 mRNA in the hhfΔ deletion strains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The levels of bound AGA1, MFA1, and MFA2 mRNAs declined by ~50%, while those of AGA2 declined even more in hhf1Δ cells.
source: This result was verified using RaPID-qPCR where the levels of bound AGA1, MFA1, and MFA2 mRNAs declined by ~50%, while those of AGA2 declined even more (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The deletion of HAT1 or SAS2 had the same reduced mating efficiency as observed with hhf1Δ cells.
source: We found that the deletion of HAT1 or SAS2 had the same reduced efficiency as observed with hhf1Δ cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpression of WT HHF1 caused a >2-fold increase in mating efficiency.
source: Overexpression of WT HHF1 caused a >2-fold increase in mating efficiency (Figure 5B), while overexpression of the K-to-R mutant abolished it.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of the K-to-R mutant abolished mating efficiency.
source: Overexpression of WT HHF1 caused a >2-fold increase in mating efficiency (Figure 5B), while overexpression of the K-to-R mutant abolished it.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of the K-to-Q mutant yielded the same twofold increase in mating efficiency as observed upon WT HHF1 overexpression.
source: Correspondingly, overexpression of the K-to-Q mutant yielded the same twofold increase in mating efficiency as observed upon WT HHF1 overexpression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of HHF1K-to-R from the genome led to a 50% decrease in mating.
source: We found that the expression of this sole copy of HHF1 led to a 50% decrease in mating (Figure 5C), but without lowering HHF1 mRNA expression (e.g., level of HHF1K-to-R=1.7 ± 0.6-fold over HHF1 in WT cells [avg. ± SEM, n = 3]).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Deletion of SCP160 prevents the polarized trafficking of mPOL mRNAs on cER, resulting in a loss in chemotropism, a 60–70% decrease in mating in heterozygous crosses, and a >98% decrease in homozygous crosses.
source: Deletion of SCP160 was shown to prevent the polarized trafficking of these mRNAs on cER, resulting in a loss in chemotropism, a 60–70% decrease in mating in heterozygous crosses, and a >98% decrease in homozygous crosses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Gelin-Licht et al., 2012).

claim: Crosses of MATα hhf1Δ cells against MATa scp160Δ cells showed a block in mating similar to that of hhf1Δ x WT crosses.
source: We crossed MATα hhf1Δ cells against MATa scp160Δ cells and observed a block in mating similar to that of hhf1Δ x WT crosses (Figure 5D), indicating that there was no additive defect when single gene mutations are present in the separate mating partners.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: hhf1Δ scp160Δ double mutants crossed against WT cells showed a complete block in mating (i.e., sterility).
source: However, when hhf1Δ scp160Δ double mutants are crossed against WT cells, we observed a complete block in mating (i.e., sterility), reminiscent of a scp160Δ homozygous cross (Gelin-Licht et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 5D and citation to previous work (Gelin-Licht et al., 2012).

claim: A single motif of 47 nucleotides is present in the coding region of all five MATa messages examined.
source: Although we anticipated that the H4 interaction site might reside (at least in part) within the 3'UTR, based on the RaPID-MS experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we identified a single motif of 47 nucleotides present in the coding region of all five MATa messages examined (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by MEME analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: AGA2 47-MUT, but not AGA2 27-MUT, led to a loss of AGA2 mRNA assembly into the mating mRNP particle.
source: When substituted for the native motif in AGA2, we found that AGA2 47-MUT, but not AGA2 27-MUT, led to a loss of AGA2 mRNA assembly into the mating mRNP particle precipitated using STE2 as the pulldown mRNA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Either motif mutation or AGA2 gene deletion resulted in significant defects in the ability of cells to mate with WT yeast.
source: Similarly, the deletion of AGA2 itself also led to defects in mating mRNP assembly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and either motif mutation or gene deletion resulted in significant defects in the ability of cells to mate with WT yeast (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 6C and RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Two distinct non-overlapping motifs of 45 and 25 bases could be identified in the MFα1, MFAα2, STE3, and SAG1 mRNAs.
source: Bioinformatic analyses revealed that this motif was not present in the mating mRNAs expressed in MATα cells; however, two distinct non-overlapping motifs of 45 and 25 bases could be identified in the MFα1, MFAα2, STE3, and SAG1 mRNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by MEME analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reduced shmoo formation was observed for both the wild-type MATα and MATa deletion strains in the non-isogenic crosses.
source: We observed reduced shmoo formation for both the wild-type MATα and MATa deletion strains in the non-isogenic crosses, as compared to the isogenic WT MATα and WT MATa cross (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by shmooing efficiency measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Deletion mutants dhh1Δ, pat1Δ, and dhh1Δ pat1Δ had no significant inhibitory effect upon mating.
source: However, unlike the previously published results (Aronov et al., 2015), we found that these same deletion mutants had no significant inhibitory effect upon mating (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mating assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Under non-inducing conditions (i.e., 2% glucose), few cells had Dhh1-mCherry puncta (2.3 ± 0.2%) and little to no co-localization between the multiple mRNAs detected and the puncta observed.
source: Under non-inducing conditions (i.e., 2% glucose), we observed few cells with Dhh1-mCherry puncta (2.3 ± 0.2%; avg. ± SEM) and little to no co-localization between the multiple mRNAs detected and the puncta observed.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: All cells formed discrete Dhh1-mCherry-labeled puncta when shifted to a no-glucose medium and 40.9 ± 5.2% co-localization with STE2 mRNA was observed.
source: In contrast, all cells formed discrete Dhh1-mCherry-labeled puncta when shifted to a no-glucose medium and we observed 40.9 ± 5.2% (avg. ± SEM) co-localization with STE2 mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Three interactions between STE2 and AGA2 were observed, consisting of ORF-ORF, ORF-5'UTR, and 3'UTR-3'UTR.
source: Importantly, we observed three interactions between STE2 and AGA2, consisting of ORF-ORF, ORF-5'UTR, and 3'UTR-3'UTR (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which were confirmed by DNA sequencing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin conformation capture (3C) data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: These interactions were not observed between STE2 and GET1, or AGA2 and DDI2, or between ASH1 and AGA2.
source: These interactions were specific, as they were not observed between STE2 and GET1, or AGA2 and DDI2, or between ASH1 and AGA2, for example (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, for example of latter).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin conformation capture (3C) data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 9.5% fully co-localized signals and 73.6% partially co-localized signals were observed between STE2 and AGA2 loci.
source: We observed 9.5% fully co-localized signals (i.e., 100% overlapping) and 73.6% partially co-localized signals (10–25% overlapping), where both loci appear adjacent to each other (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by live cell fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Only 17.3% of the STE2 and AGA2 loci were not closely associated.
source: In contrast, only 17.3% of the loci were not closely associated.
evidence: This is supported by live cell fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Far less locus co-localization or adjacent loci (e.g., 2.3 and 27.2%, respectively) were observed between AGA2 and ASH1 as compared to AGA2 and STE2.
source: As a control, we performed live imaging of AGA2 224 × TetR and the ASH1 gene tagged with 256 × LacO repeats and the abovementioned fluorescent reporters (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D), and observed far less locus co-localization or adjacent loci (e.g., 2.3 and 27.2%, respectively), as compared to AGA2 224 × TetR and STE2 256 × LacO (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by live cell fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Treatment with 1,10 phenanthroline resulted in a modest increase (40–50%) in non-co-localized AGA2 and STE2 alleles.
source: Next, to determine if the allele interaction is transcription-mediated, we treated AGA2 224 × TetR- and STE2 256 × LacO-tagged cells with 1,10 phenanthroline, which inhibits general transcription. We observed a modest increase (40–50%) in non-co-localized AGA2 and STE2 alleles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), which suggests that allele apposition may be mediated by transcription.
evidence: This is supported by live cell fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The deletion of HHF1 alone reduced the level of allelic coupling in AGA2 224 × TetR and STE2 256 × LacO cells.
source: Likewise, the deletion of HHF1 alone reduced the level of allelic coupling in AGA2 224 × TetR and STE2 256 × LacO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), which could indicate a structural role for H4 in leading to RNA multiplexing.
evidence: This is supported by live cell fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The mRNAs of HSP genes previously shown to undergo intergenic interaction (e.g., TMA10, HSP12, HSP82, SSA2, and SSA4) were found to co-precipitate both before, but much more after heat shock.
source: Importantly, the mRNAs of HSP genes previously shown to undergo intergenic interaction (e.g., TMA10, HSP12, HSP82, SSA2, and SSA4) (Chowdhary et al., 2019) were found to co-precipitate both before, but much more after heat shock (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 8A and citation to previous work (Chowdhary et al., 2019).

claim: Under non-heat shock conditions, 30.4 ± 0.9% of HSP104 mRNA co-localized with SSA2 mRNA, whereas this increased to 76.8 ± 0.5% upon heat shock.
source: Under non-heat shock conditions, we found that 30.4 ± 0.9% of HSP104 mRNA co-localized with SSA2 mRNA, whereas this increased to 76.8 ± 0.5% (avg. ± SEM) upon heat shock (Figure 8B and C; representative images shown in Figure 8B and quantified in Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Similar low levels of STE2 co-localization with SSA2 mRNA were found either with or without heat shock (11.9 ± 0.5% and 11.7 ± 0.4%, respectively).
source: As a control, we visualized STE2 mRNA in co-localization experiments with SSA2 mRNA. We found similar low levels of STE2 co-localization with SSA2 mRNA either with or without heat shock (11.9 ± 0.5% and 11.7 ± 0.4%, respectively) (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Three potential motifs were identified in HSP gene sequences.
source: We examined the HSP gene sequences for recognizable motifs and identified three potential motifs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) present in nearly all HSP cohort genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MEME analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Single gene deletions did not affect doubling time after heat shock.
source: While single gene deletions did not affect doubling time after heat shock (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells treated with 3-IAA showed a longer doubling time after heat shock (at all times examined), as compared to WT cells or untreated AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells treated with 3-IAA showed a longer doubling time after heat shock (at all times examined), as compared to WT cells or untreated AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells.
source: While single gene deletions did not affect doubling time after heat shock (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells treated with 3-IAA showed a longer doubling time after heat shock (at all times examined), as compared to WT cells or untreated AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HSP mRNA multiplexing with HSP104 mRNA was reduced significantly in AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells after heat shock in the presence of 3-IAA.
source: Moreover, we found that HSP mRNA (e.g., TMA10, HSP12, HSP82, SSA2, and SSA4) multiplexing with HSP104 mRNA was reduced significantly in these cells after heat shock in the presence of 3-IAA (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Upon heat shock, reduced mRNA co-localization was observed in AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells either with (51.5 ± 0.9%) or without (55.8 ± 0.9%) the addition of 3-IAA, as compared to WT cells (76.8 ± 0.5%).
source: Upon heat shock, we observed reduced mRNA co-localization in AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells either with (51.5 ± 0.9%; avg. ± SEM) or without (55.8 ± 0.9%; avg. ± SEM) the addition of 3-IAA, as compared to WT cells (76.8 ± 0.5%).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The pulldown of UGO1 mRNA led to co-precipitation of cohort MOMP mRNAs (e.g., TOM5, TOM6, TOM22), but not GAPDH mRNA.
source: The pulldown of UGO1 mRNA led to co-precipitation of cohort MOMP mRNAs (e.g., TOM5, TOM6, TOM22; Figure 9A), but not GAPDH mRNA, suggesting that a specific mRNA multiplex can be detected.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: STE2 mRNA could co-precipitate with UGO1 mRNA.
source: Since we initially observed co-precipitation of the mating mRNAs along with OM45 (Figure 1A and B), which codes for another MOMP, we examined for the precipitation of STE2 mRNA with UGO1 mRNA. Indeed, STE2 mRNA could co-precipitate with UGO1 mRNA, suggesting a possible interaction between MOMP and mating pathway mRNA complexes.
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 46.3 ± 1.7% of PP7-tagged TOM6 mRNA co-localized with MS2-tagged UGO1 mRNA.
source: We found that 46.3 ± 1.7% (avg. ± SEM) of PP7-tagged TOM6 mRNA co-localized with MS2-tagged UGO1 mRNA (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: 7.7 ± 1.1% of HSP104 mRNA co-localized with PP7-tagged TOM6 mRNA.
source: As control, we visualized native HSP104 mRNA in co-localization experiments with PP7-tagged TOM6 mRNA using smFISH. We found 7.7 ± 1.1% of HSP104 mRNA co-localized with PP7-tagged TOM6 mRNA (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: RaPID pulldown of STE5 mRNA after pheromone induction led to a significant co-precipitation of FUS3 mRNA, although only slight, but significant, increases in STE7 or STE11 mRNA pulldown were detected.
source: RaPID pulldown of STE5 mRNA after pheromone induction led to a significant co-precipitation of FUS3 mRNA, although only slight, but significant, increases in STE7 or STE11 mRNA pulldown were detected (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by RaPID-qPCR data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: 19.6 ± 1.4% co-localization was observed between MS2-tagged FUS3 and PP7-tagged STE5 mRNA in the presence of α-factor.
source: We verified the association of MS2-tagged FUS3 and PP7-tagged STE5 mRNA in cells using smFISH and observed 19.6 ± 1.4% (avg. ± SEM) co-localization in the presence of α-factor (Figure 9E and F).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 9E and F.

claim: Only 3.2 ± 0.6% co-localization was found between HSP104 mRNA and PP7-tagged FUS3 mRNA.
source: As a control, we visualized HSP104 mRNA co-localization with PP7-tagged FUS3 mRNA, but found only 3.2 ± 0.6% co-localization (Figure 9E and F).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 9E and F.

claim: Eukaryotes have preferentially relied on the discontiguous distribution of genes over different chromosomes due to greater complexity observed both at the gene and cellular levels.
source: Perhaps due to the greater complexity observed both at the gene and cellular levels, eukaryotes have preferentially relied on the discontiguous distribution of genes over different chromosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about eukaryotic genome organization.

claim: The co-regulation of gene expression presumably becomes dependent on shared transcriptional control elements and specific RBPs that interact selectively with certain transcripts and confer trafficking to sites of co-translation.
source: In this case, the co-regulation of gene expression presumably becomes dependent on shared transcriptional control elements and specific RBPs that interact selectively with certain transcripts and confer trafficking to sites of co-translation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms of gene co-regulation in eukaryotes.

claim: mRNAs encoding secreted proteins involved in mating multiplex into a functionally selective mRNP complex – the mating transperon.
source: Since a corresponding complex (e.g., STE2, AGA1, AGA2, MFA1, MFA2) could also be precipitated from MATa cells, it suggested to us that mRNAs encoding secreted proteins involved in mating (e.g., pheromones, pheromone receptors, agglutinins, and proteases) multiplex into a functionally selective mRNP complex – the mating transperon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RaPID-seq and RaPID-qPCR data from both MATα and MATa cells.

claim: Interallelic coupling may give rise to RNA multiplexing.
source: Importantly, a specific interaction between the STE2 and AGA2 genes was identified in MATa cells, which suggests that interallelic coupling may give rise to RNA multiplexing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on chromatin conformation capture and live cell imaging data.

claim: Allele apposition may be mediated by transcription.
source: We observed a modest increase (40–50%) in non-co-localized AGA2 and STE2 alleles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), which suggests that allele apposition may be mediated by transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the effect of transcription inhibitor treatment on allelic coupling.

claim: H4 may have a structural role in leading to RNA multiplexing.
source: Likewise, the deletion of HHF1 alone reduced the level of allelic coupling in AGA2 224 × TetR and STE2 256 × LacO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), which could indicate a structural role for H4 in leading to RNA multiplexing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the effect of HHF1 deletion on allelic coupling.

claim: Eukaryotic mRNP complexes/transperons are the functional equivalents of bacterial operons.
source: To the best of our knowledge, the results presented here support the concept that eukaryotic mRNP complexes/transperons are the functional equivalents of bacterial operons, as first proposed by Keene, 2007 and Keene and Tenenbaum, 2002.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the integration of all experimental findings and citations to previous proposals (Keene, 2007; Keene and Tenenbaum, 2002).

claim: Eukaryotes may circumvent polycistronicity by assembling relevant mRNAs into functional complexes that confer co-translation.
source: Thus, eukaryotes may circumvent polycistronicity by assembling relevant mRNAs into functional complexes that confer co-translation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: mRNA assembly into functional transperons occurs via physical intergenic interactions that couple individual alleles concurrent with transcription.
source: This is likely to occur via physical intergenic interactions that couple individual alleles concurrent with transcription to form transperons that can undergo export and translation at different sites within the cell (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the integration of chromatin capture, RNA multiplexing, and localization data.
